mean: to make someone believe that something is true or right
ex: It took Meera a whole evening to convince her father that a BCom graduate can become a good chef.
note: Convince = make someone believe; persuade = make someone act. 'She convinced me it was safe, then persuaded me to go.'
ex2: It took three test rides to convince Gurpreet that an electric scooter could climb the slopes of Shimla.

mean: to disagree with a plan or idea and try to stop it
ex: Residents of the Pune colony met on Sunday to oppose the plan to cut forty old banyan trees for a parking lot.
note: Say 'I oppose the plan' or 'I am opposed to the plan', never 'I oppose to the plan'.
ex2: Several parents oppose the school's plan to start classes at seven o'clock in the middle of a Delhi winter.

mean: to agree, often unwillingly, that something is true
ex: Vikram had to admit that his sister's route to Lonavala was faster than his.
note: Use -ing after it: 'He admitted copying' or 'admitted to copying'. It also means let in: 'admitted to hospital'.
ex2: The shopkeeper in Chandni Chowk would not admit that the 'pure silk' saree was mostly polyester.

mean: to give good reasons why something is right or needed
ex: How will the school justify a thirty per cent fee hike when half the classrooms still have no working fans?
note: Something that 'cannot be justified' has no good defence at all. Noun: justification.
ex2: Can you justify spending two lakh rupees on a phone when your laptop is falling apart?

mean: a discussion where people give opposite views on a question
ex: The college debate on open-book exams got so heated that the principal had to step in.
note: Noun: 'a debate on/about X'. Verb takes no preposition: 'we debated the issue', not 'debated on the issue'.
ex2: The debate in the newsroom was whether to lead the front page with the flood story or the cricket win.

mean: based on good reasons, so it should be accepted
ex: Lata aunty's point in the family WhatsApp group was valid: the forwarded 'cure' had no doctor's name on it.
note: It also means officially usable: a valid ticket, a valid passport. The 'validity' of a phone recharge is the same sense.
ex2: The third umpire ruled the catch valid because the fielder's foot never touched the boundary rope.

mean: to answer an argument or attack with one of your own
ex: When the manager blamed her team for the delay, Tanvi was ready to counter with the client's late approvals.
note: Common in nouns like 'counter-argument' and 'counter-offer'. 'Counterproductive' means it works against your own goal.
ex2: When Dadi said girls shouldn't ride motorbikes, Aisha was quick to counter that Dadi had once driven a tractor.

mean: so strong or interesting that you have to believe it or pay attention
ex: The lawyer showed compelling evidence that the signatures on the land papers in Jabalpur were forged.
note: A 'compelling story' is one you can't stop reading. 'Compulsive' is different: unable to stop yourself (a compulsive liar).
ex2: The first half of the film is slow, but the courtroom scenes make a compelling case for watching it to the end.

mean: a reason you give for not agreeing with something
ex: Nobody at the housing society meeting raised an objection to repainting the building before the monsoon.
note: You have an objection 'to' something, not 'on' it. An NOC is a No Objection Certificate.
ex2: Nanaji's only objection to the wedding menu was that it had no puran poli.

mean: to get someone to do something by giving them good reasons
ex: Jaspreet tried for weeks to persuade her grandmother to get the cataract surgery at the free eye camp.
note: Persuade someone TO DO something; convince someone THAT something is true. Pronounced pur-SWAYD, with a 'w' sound.
ex2: No salesman could persuade Mr D'Souza to swap his twenty-year-old Fiat for a shiny new car.

mean: the opinion you openly hold on an issue
ex: The coach took a firm stance: no player who skipped practice would play the Ranji match.
note: Also a batter's way of standing at the crease; picture the cricket stance to remember 'where you stand'.
ex2: The resident welfare association has not yet taken a stance on letting delivery riders use the lift.

mean: to say the opposite of what someone said, or to not match it
ex: The CCTV footage seemed to contradict the shopkeeper's claim that the thief had come after midnight.
note: Facts can contradict each other too: 'The two reports contradict each other.' Adjective: contradictory.
ex2: Children in the joint family quickly learn not to contradict Nanaji at the dinner table.

mean: to admit, often unwillingly, that the other side is right or has won
ex: After the third recount, the losing candidate in the village panchayat election had to concede defeat.
note: Cricket uses it too: 'the bowler conceded 40 runs'. Conceding a small point makes your main argument look fairer, not weaker.
ex2: Even Kunal's fiercest critics had to concede that his century had saved the match.

mean: to prove that a claim is wrong
ex: The fact-checker used the bank's own circular to refute the viral claim that all ATMs would shut for a week.
note: Refute = prove wrong; rebut = argue against (may not succeed); deny = just say it's false. Don't use 'refute' when you mean 'deny'.
ex2: The science teacher used a simple kitchen experiment to refute the old belief that mixing fish and milk is poisonous.

mean: to slowly weaken something, often in a hidden way
ex: Repeated paper leaks undermine public trust in the state's board exams.
note: Usually slow or hidden damage. Don't confuse with 'underestimate' (to think something is smaller or weaker than it is).
ex2: Checking every line of her work will only undermine the new intern's confidence.

mean: to support a claim with proof
ex: The insurance company asked Farhan to substantiate his claim with the hospital bills and discharge summary.
note: 'Unsubstantiated' means not backed by proof, common in news: 'unsubstantiated rumours'.
ex2: The reporter could not substantiate the rumour about the film star's secret wedding, so she dropped the story.

mean: able to be believed or trusted
ex: The reporter would not run the story until she found a credible source inside the hospital.
note: Credible = believable; credulous = too quick to believe; creditable = deserving praise. 'Incredible' now usually just means amazing.
ex2: After five losses in a row, the team's claim to be title favourites no longer sounds credible.

mean: a warning or condition you add to what you say
ex: The doctor approved Papa's Kedarnath trek with one caveat: he must carry his inhaler at all times.
note: Pronounced KAV-ee-at, not ka-VEET. 'Caveat emptor' (Latin) means 'let the buyer beware'.
ex2: The landlord agreed to let the students keep a pet, with one caveat: it had to be smaller than a cat.

mean: to argue against a claim by giving reasons it is wrong
ex: In the inter-college debate, Nikhil had just two minutes to rebut every point the other team made.
note: Rebut = answer with counter-arguments; refute = actually prove wrong. Noun: rebuttal. Stress the second syllable: ri-BUT.
ex2: The company issued a press note to rebut reports that it was shutting down its Coimbatore factory.

mean: to say firmly that something is true, especially in an argument
ex: The farmers contend that the new canal will flood their fields every monsoon.
note: 'Contend with' means deal with a difficulty: 'contend with Mumbai traffic'. A 'contender' is someone competing for a prize.
ex2: Some tourism experts contend that cheaper train tickets would bring many more visitors to the North-East.

mean: clear, logical and convincing
ex: Priya's cogent two-page note persuaded the hostel warden to keep the library open till midnight.
note: Soft 'g', as in 'gem': KOH-junt. Cogent praises the logic; compelling can also mean emotionally gripping.
ex2: The class monitor gave a cogent reason for moving the picnic: the bus company had suddenly doubled its rates.

mean: impossible to prove wrong
ex: Hawk-Eye gave irrefutable proof that the ball had pitched outside leg stump.
note: Two pronunciations are accepted: i-ri-FYOO-tuh-bul and i-REF-yuh-tuh-bul. Use it only when the proof really is final.
ex2: The bank statement was irrefutable proof that the money had gone into the wrong account.

mean: open to argument, or no longer worth arguing about because things changed
ex: Whether to fly or take the Shatabdi became a moot point once every flight to Bhopal was cancelled.
note: UK: 'moot point' = still debatable; US: no longer relevant. Indian news uses 'mooted' = proposed. Never 'mute point'.
ex2: Whether to hold the Holi party on the terrace or in the park became moot when the rain started.

mean: language used to persuade, often impressive but empty
ex: Voters in the small town were tired of election rhetoric and just wanted to know when the water tank would be fixed.
note: Silent 'h': RET-uh-rik. Neutral sense: the art of persuasive speaking. A 'rhetorical question' expects no answer.
ex2: Behind the founder's rhetoric about changing the world, the startup still had not paid its interns.

mean: a twisted, weaker version of someone's argument, attacked instead of the real one
ex: 'So you want students never to study?' was a straw man; Ishaan had only asked for fewer Saturday classes.
note: The fair opposite is 'steelmanning': stating the other side's strongest version before you reply to it.
ex2: Saying that people who want cleaner footpaths 'hate street food' is a straw man; nobody asked to ban the vendors.

mean: seeming right at first, but actually false or misleading
ex: The cream's specious claim to remove dark circles in three days fooled half the girls in the hostel.
note: Don't confuse with 'spacious' (roomy). Like 'plausible', but suggesting the appearance of truth is a trick.
ex2: The agent's specious warning that flat prices would double next month pushed the young couple in Pune to buy in a hurry.

mean: to say something is true, often without giving proof
ex: Many coaching centres claim that most of their students crack JEE on the first attempt.
ex2: The fielder continued to claim the catch, but the replay showed the ball had bounced first.
note: A claim may not be true, which is why news reports say 'he claimed'. Also a noun: 'an insurance claim'.

mean: to say that something is not true
ex: The cricket board was quick to deny reports that the captain would step down after the series.
ex2: Chotu's face was covered in chocolate, yet he continued to deny eating the last eclair.
note: Deny + -ing: 'he denied taking it', not 'denied to take'. 'Deny someone a visa' means refuse to give it.

mean: to show with facts that something is true
ex: The bill from the Bengaluru showroom was enough to prove that Divya had bought the phone before the price drop.
ex2: The young striker from Manipur had one match to prove that she belonged in the national team.
note: The noun is 'proof', not 'prove': 'Do you have proof?' Past participle: proved or proven.

mean: a serious disagreement or argument, often a long one
ex: The dispute between the two brothers over their father's land in Bihar dragged on for eleven years.
ex2: A dispute over a no-ball in the last over held up the gully cricket final for twenty minutes.
note: Also a verb: 'Nobody disputes the facts.' Indian news often says 'property dispute' and 'border dispute'.

mean: an agreement where each side gives up a little
ex: After an hour of arguing, the family reached a compromise: biryani on Saturday, dosa on Sunday.
ex2: The workers and the factory owners in Kanpur finally agreed on a compromise over night-shift pay.
note: As a verb it can also mean put at risk: 'Don't compromise safety.' Context tells you which sense.

mean: to say publicly that you support or approve of something
ex: Doctors at the conference refused to endorse the herbal powder until it had been properly tested.
ex2: Fans were surprised to see their favourite footballer endorse a sugary cold drink on billboards.
note: Celebrities 'endorse' products in ads, which is called an 'endorsement'. You also endorse a cheque by signing its back.

mean: to decide that an idea is not worth thinking about
ex: Don't dismiss Riya's idea just because she is the youngest person on the team.
ex2: The high court decided to dismiss the petition because it had been filed two years too late.
note: Also means send away or sack: 'dismissed from service'. In cricket, a batter is dismissed when out.

mean: to say something firmly and confidently
ex: At the society meeting, Mrs Rao stood up to assert that the parking rules applied to everyone, including the secretary.
ex2: The young umpire had to assert his authority when both captains crowded around him.
note: 'Assert yourself' means speak up confidently for yourself. 'Assertive' is confident, not rude; 'aggressive' is rude.

mean: to agree with an opinion, usually in a formal way
ex: Both doctors at the Vellore hospital concur that the knee surgery can wait six months.
ex2: Most commentators would concur that it was the finest spell of swing bowling seen at Lord's in years.
note: Formal; common in courts and meetings. Say 'concur with someone' and 'concur on something'.

mean: showing very strong feeling, especially when against something
ex: Fishermen in Kerala raised vehement objections to the plan to build a port on their beach.
ex2: Despite Ammi's vehement protests, Zoya cut her long hair short before starting college.
note: The 'h' is silent: VEE-uh-munt. The adverb is very common: 'vehemently opposed'.

mean: to make two opposite ideas fit together, or make people friends again
ex: Kiran found it hard to reconcile her uncle's speeches about honesty with the way he dodged his taxes.
ex2: It took the two cousins three years to reconcile after the quarrel at their grandmother's birthday.
note: Two uses: reconcile ideas (make them fit) and reconcile people (become friends again). Noun: reconciliation.

mean: impossible to defend or to keep going
ex: Once the hotel bill turned up, Karan's claim that he had stayed home all weekend became untenable.
ex2: With the rent doubling every year, life in the Bandra flat became untenable for the young couple.
note: Used for arguments and for situations: 'the situation became untenable' means it could not go on.

mean: pretending to be honest or innocent while hiding the truth
ex: It is disingenuous of the builder to blame the rain when he started the flats three years late.
ex2: The batter's claim that he hadn't felt the ball touch his glove seemed disingenuous to everyone watching.
note: Nothing to do with 'ingenious' (clever). Disingenuous means slyly insincere.

mean: attacking the person instead of answering their argument
ex: Calling the young professor 'a kid' was an ad hominem attack; nobody answered her data on Delhi's air.
ex2: The debate judge cut marks from the team that made ad hominem remarks about the other speaker's accent.
note: Latin for 'to the person'. On TV debates it is the commonest way to dodge a point.

mean: a statement that does not follow logically from what came before
ex: 'He is tall, so he must be good at maths' is a non sequitur that made the whole staff room laugh.
ex2: Asked about the potholes, the contractor's reply about his daughter's wedding was a complete non sequitur.
instead: has nothing to do with it
note: Latin for 'it does not follow'. Also used for a random remark that has nothing to do with the topic.

mean: a strong written or spoken attack on an idea or person
ex: The retired judge's new book is a polemic against the slow pace of trials in Indian courts.
ex2: Instead of a balanced review, the film critic wrote a two-page polemic against Bollywood remakes.
note: Adjective: polemical. A polemic argues one side hard; it does not try to be balanced.
